At the height of the trade war between Trump and China, when tariffs seemed to rise almost every week, companies like Logitech quickly responded with substantial price hikes on their US products.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. Yet no company appears to have passed any of that money back to consumers, and a class action lawsuit is now seeking to address the situation…

The Trump Tariff Saga

Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China last year, apparently believing that slapping higher tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to shift their manufacturing back to the US.

That was never going to happen. The US lacks the production infrastructure, expertise, and cheap labour needed to support consumer electronics manufacturing at the scale major brands require.

Trump has consistently claimed that tariffs would be paid by China, but in reality these costs are borne by US brands importing finished goods, with the added expense ultimately passed on to consumers through higher prices. At the height of the saga, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Logitech, for example, raised prices on roughly half its product range by up to 25%.

Consumers Are Owed Refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that payments made by US businesses must be returned. The refund process is currently underway.

The issue is that these costs were effectively borne by consumers through higher product prices, and no affected company has yet signalled any intention to refund its customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class action against Logitech, demanding refunds for consumers who paid inflated prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac Opinion

The principle here is indisputable. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and the government is now refunding them. Morally, they should return the tariff-related portion of the product price to consumers who purchased during that period.

Enforcing it, however, would be enormously challenging. Logitech would need to identify every transaction made through its vast network of third-party retailers, track what consumers paid, and calculate the tariff component within that.

If the lawsuit succeeds, it would set a fascinating precedent — though we should note that it's only the lawyers who typically make a killing from class actions, with the average payout to consumers usually being quite small.
